report:
### Conclusion
The health claim is **true**. Clinical trial evidence and clinical practice guidelines confirm that exemestane significantly reduces the incidence of invasive breast cancer in postmenopausal women at elevated risk.

### Summary of Evidence
The evidence supporting this claim comes primarily from the landmark Phase III Mammary Prevention Trial (MAP.3). In this double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, daily administration of 25 mg of exemestane reduced the relative incidence of invasive breast cancer by 65% in high-risk postmenopausal women over a median follow-up of three years [https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/Nejmoa1103507]. 

Major healthcare and research institutions endorse these findings:
- The **National Cancer Institute (NCI)** highlights clinical trial results showing that exemestane substantially reduces invasive breast cancer risk in postmenopausal women with elevated risk factors [https://www.cancer.gov/types/breast/research/exemestane-reduces-risk].
- The **U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF)** recommends clinicians offer risk-reducing medications—specifically including aromatase inhibitors such as exemestane—to postmenopausal women at increased risk for breast cancer who are at low risk for severe adverse medication effects [https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/breast-cancer-medications-for-risk-reduction].

While potential side effects (such as impacts on bone density) must be weighed against individual benefit, scientific consensus supports exemestane's efficacy in lowering primary breast cancer incidence in this population.

### Sources

- https://www.cancer.gov/types/breast/research/exemestane-reduces-risk
- https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/breast-cancer-medications-for-risk-reduction
